h1: Biological Age Calculator: Your Fitness Age
capsule: Your fitness age is the age of an average healthy person with the same aerobic fitness (VO2max) as you. This calculator estimates your VO2max with the published HUNT model from Norway — age, sex, waist, resting heart rate and how you exercise — and compares it with measured norms. It's a science-based estimate of one part of biological age, not a lab test or a medical diagnosis.

disclaimer: Educational estimate, not a medical test or diagnosis. The reference norms come from healthy, fairly active Norwegian volunteers, so many people land a little older than their age. What matters is the direction: more regular hard exercise, a smaller waist and a lower resting heart rate all move your fitness age down.

sections.h2: What is biological age — and what is fitness age?
sections.body: Biological age describes how old your body behaves rather than how many birthdays you've had. There is no single measure of it: epigenetic clocks read DNA methylation, others use blood tests. Fitness age is one well-studied part of it: it compares your cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max) with the average healthy person of each age. It matters because fitness is one of the strongest predictors of long-term health — in a study of 122,007 patients (Mandsager 2018), people with the lowest fitness had much higher mortality than the fittest, with no upper limit to the benefit. Unlike a DNA test, your fitness age can change within weeks of training.

sections.h2: How this fitness age calculator works
sections.body: It uses the non-exercise model from the HUNT Fitness Study in Norway (Nes 2011), in which healthy adults ran a treadmill test to exhaustion. The researchers found that age, waist circumference, resting heart rate and a physical-activity index predict measured VO2max well. The activity index multiplies three answers: how often you exercise, how hard, and for how long. Your estimated VO2max is then compared with the average VO2max of healthy men or women at each age from the same study (Loe 2013) — the age where that average matches yours is your fitness age. In a follow-up of about 37,000 people over 24 years, this estimate predicted mortality (Nes 2014).

sections.h2: How to lower your fitness age
sections.body: The biggest lever is exercise intensity: in the model, sessions that leave you breathless and sweaty count twice as much as easy ones, and near-exhaustion efforts three times. Adding one or two interval sessions a week (for example 4 × 4 minutes hard with easy recovery) and building steady Zone 2 cardio raises VO2max within 6–12 weeks. A smaller waist and a lower resting heart rate follow from the same training plus better sleep and less alcohol. Guides: [Zone 2 training](/articles/zone-2-training-aerobic-base), [how to increase VO2max](/articles/vo2max-increase-aerobic-engine) and [resting heart rate by age](/tools/resting-heart-rate).

sections.h2: What is a good VO2max for my age?
sections.body: In the HUNT study of 3,816 healthy adults (Loe 2013), average measured VO2max was about 54 ml/kg/min for men in their 20s, 49 in their 30s, 47 in their 40s, 43 in their 50s, 39 in their 60s and 35 from 70; for women about 43, 40, 38, 34, 31 and 28. VO2max falls by about 8% per decade after 50, but active people keep much higher values. Wearables such as Apple Watch, Garmin and Oura also estimate VO2max; their numbers differ from this model and from a lab test, so compare each source only with itself. More: [VO2max calculator](/tools/vo2max).

faqTitle: Biological age and fitness age — common questions

faq.a: Your VO2max is estimated with the HUNT model (Nes 2011) from age, sex, waist, resting heart rate and exercise habits. Your fitness age is the age at which the average healthy person of your sex has the same VO2max (Loe 2013 norms).

faq.q: Is fitness age the same as biological age?
faq.a: No. Fitness age measures one part of biological age — aerobic fitness. Other methods use DNA methylation (epigenetic clocks) or blood tests. Fitness age is one of the most practical parts because it predicts long-term health and you can change it with training.
It's an estimate: the model explains about 60% of the differences in measured VO2max, so your real value can be several points higher or lower. Only a lab or treadmill test measures VO2max directly.

faq.q: Why is my fitness age older than my real age?
faq.a: The reference norms come from healthy, fairly active volunteers, so the bar is high. Low exercise intensity, a larger waist and a higher resting heart rate push the estimate up — all three can be improved.

faq.q: How can I lower my fitness age?
faq.a: Add harder sessions that leave you breathless (such as intervals) to regular aerobic training, reduce waist size and improve sleep. VO2max usually rises within 6–12 weeks of consistent training.

faq.q: What is a good VO2max for my age?
faq.a: Average healthy values (Loe 2013): men about 54 ml/kg/min in their 20s, 47 in their 40s and 39 in their 60s; women about 43, 38 and 31. Higher is better.

methodology: Estimated VO2max = 100.27 − 0.296×age − 0.369×waist(cm) − 0.155×resting HR + 0.226×PA-index for men, and 74.74 − 0.247×age − 0.259×waist − 0.114×resting HR + 0.198×PA-index for women (Nes 2011). The PA-index multiplies frequency (0, 1, 2.5 or 5), intensity (1, 2 or 3) and duration (0.1, 0.38, 0.75 or 1) scores from the HUNT questionnaire (Nauman 2012). Fitness age is read from the mean measured VO2max of healthy men and women by decade (Loe 2013), interpolated between decades. The original model used a seated resting heart rate; a watch's resting heart rate is usually a little lower, which slightly improves the estimate. Educational estimate, not a diagnosis.
sourcesContributes: The equations used here: estimated VO2max from age, waist circumference, resting heart rate and a physical-activity index, developed and validated in healthy adults of the Norwegian HUNT study.
